headline: The Quant Cookbook: 151 Recipes, No Restaurant
lede: A 361-page paper purporting to unlock every hedge-fund algorithm has circulated again on finance X with the predictable rush of engagement. It is a real and useful reference work — just not the arsenal the tweet suggests.
body:
The document is genuine. Zura Kakushadze, a Georgian-American physicist turned quant formerly at Bank of America and Merrill Lynch, and Juan Andrés Serur, of Argentina's Universidad del CEMA, released the preprint in October 2018 on SSRN and arXiv. Palgrave Macmillan published it as a book the same year. The paper runs to 361 pages in its preprint form and catalogs 151 strategies — statistical arbitrage, momentum, carry, volatility targeting, options spreads, convertible-bond trades, cryptocurrency pairs — each sketched with mathematical formulas and pointers to the academic literature. It is, by any fair measure, the most comprehensive taxonomy of publicly documented quantitative strategies available in a single document.

What the paper is not is a trading system. A taxonomy is not a thesis. The authors themselves are careful on this point: they provide formulas and references, not calibrated parameters. The difference matters enormously in practice. A moving-average crossover rule needs a lookback window, a position-sizing rule, a stop-loss level, a transaction-cost model, and a set of instruments — none of which are in the paper. The source code included is illustrative: it demonstrates how one might run an out-of-sample backtest (a test on data deliberately withheld during model construction, to check whether a strategy was merely fit to history) rather than providing code ready for a live brokerage connection. A mechanic's manual describes how an engine works; it does not tell you which races you will win.

The graver problem is the claim that the paper

Proprietary alpha — excess return generated by a strategy uncorrelated with broad market moves — is, by definition, not published. The strategies in the survey that work in the current market are precisely the ones sophisticated managers have kept out of journals. What does get published tends to decay: Campbell Harvey, Yan Liu, and Caroline Zhu documented in a widely cited 2016 paper that the majority of academic finance factors fail to hold up out-of-sample, in part because researchers iterate over the same historical datasets until something fits — a methodological hazard known as data-mining bias (the inflation of apparent performance when many candidate strategies are tried on the same data and only winning variants are reported). A list of 151 documented strategies is, in part, a list of strategies the market has already had years to arbitrage.

None of this makes the work valueless. For a student entering quantitative finance, Kakushadze and Serur's survey is a genuinely useful map. It covers asset classes that most introductory texts ignore — distressed debt, infrastructure, weather derivatives, tax arbitrage — and its 2,000-odd bibliographic citations point toward primary sources that repay serious study. The machine-learning entries (k-nearest neighbors, or k-NN, a classification algorithm that predicts an outcome by finding the k most similar historical observations; naive Bayes, a probabilistic classifier that assumes features are independent; and artificial neural networks) are brief but honestly framed as representative rather than exhaustive. For a practitioner building institutional knowledge or designing a research agenda, having all these strategy families in one reference is convenient, and the glossary of over 900 definitions stands on its own as a resource.

The tweet, though, is selling something the paper does not deliver. Hedge funds — at least the ones generating uncorrelated returns — are not running strategies that appear in open-access preprints. Their edge lives in execution infrastructure, proprietary data, and the continuous research effort required to stay ahead of the crowd. A library card grants access to cookbooks; it does not make a Michelin-starred chef. The paper is a library card.

concepts.definition: The portion of a portfolio's return that cannot be explained by exposure to broad market movements or other systematic risk factors. A strategy generates alpha when it earns more than its risk would predict. True alpha is rare, erodes when widely adopted, and — by definition — is not published in freely available papers, since disclosure invites competition that arbitrages it away.

A testing method in which a trading model is calibrated on one historical period (the in-sample window) and evaluated on a separate, later period that was withheld during calibration. The distinction matters because a model can always be tuned to fit past data perfectly; the out-of-sample test checks whether the apparent pattern was genuine or merely an artifact of overfitting to a particular historical episode.

The inflation of a strategy's apparent historical performance that results from testing many candidate rules on the same dataset and reporting only the best-performing ones. Also called multiple-testing bias or p-hacking. Because any finite dataset contains random patterns, an exhaustive search will always produce strategies that 'worked' in the past by chance. Campbell Harvey and co-authors estimated in 2016 that the t-ratio threshold for credible factor discovery should be raised from the conventional 2.0 to at least 3.0 to account for this effect.

books.title: 151 Trading Strategies
books.author: Zura Kakushadze & Juan Andrés Serur
books.summary: A 480-page survey published by Palgrave Macmillan in 2018 and simultaneously released as a free preprint on SSRN and arXiv. The book catalogs over 150 quantitative trading strategies across equities, options, fixed income, futures, FX, cryptocurrencies, volatility, real estate, and exotic asset classes, with more than 550 mathematical formulas and roughly 2,000 bibliographic references. It includes illustrative source code for out-of-sample backtesting and a 900-entry glossary. The work is explicitly a descriptive taxonomy and educational reference, not a source of calibrated, trade-ready signals; the authors make no performance claims for any included strategy.

fact_check: The tweet's framing — 'unlocks every algorithm used by hedge funds' — is materially misleading. The paper is a survey of publicly documented strategies, not a disclosure of proprietary hedge-fund methods; genuine alpha by definition does not appear in open-access preprints. Having the mathematical formula for a strategy does not confer the execution infrastructure, calibrated parameters, transaction-cost model, or live data feeds required to trade it profitably. The paper itself makes no profitability claims, and academic evidence from Harvey, Liu, and Zhu (2016) suggests the majority of published trading factors fail out-of-sample. The document is a legitimate and useful reference work, but the post significantly overstates what possessing it achieves.
